utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, please, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues Ms. McHenry Mr. Turone and Mr. Huber for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have the appearances from the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Edina Residovic appearing on behalf of Mr. Zejnil Delalic along with my colleague Professor Eugene O'Sullivan from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I'm Tomislav Kuzmanovic. With me is Nico Duric representing Mr. Zdravko Mucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I'm Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo appearing together with Thomas Moran on behalf of Mr. Hazim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I'm Cynthia McMurrey, and along with my colleague Ms. Nancy Boler, we represent Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Nancy Boler is not there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honours, she just stepped out of the courtroom, momentarily, to set-up an appointment. She will be right back. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I call the witness, may I give you some information? After yesterday's hearing, in view of the speed with which the witnesses are appearing, the Defence of Mr. Zejnil Delalic has done its best to ensure some more witnesses for this week. You are certainly aware that bringing witnesses from Bosnia is a difficult undertaking and any change in the order, of course, is difficult. On the list of witnesses are two witnesses under pseudonyms B and C, who are living and working in Vienna. We contacted them yesterday and they are ready to arrange with their employers whether they can travel this morning, and they will confirm by midday whether they will be able to come on Friday, in which case we would have two more witnesses to hear on Friday. That is the best we were able to do following your instructions and to contribute to the greater expediency of the proceedings. If you approve of this proposal of ours because these two witnesses were not on the list for this week. As soon as they confirm their arrival, I would give their names to my colleagues in the Defence as well as my learned friend the Prosecution, and I also wish to inform the court that these witnesses will not require protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your effort in cooperating. I think the error was because you mis-timed the length of each of the witnesses and also you assumed that the repetitious nature of the evidence would not matter at all. I think in the interest of everyone, if you try and provide for at least ten of your witnesses every week, because my understanding of it is that the responsibility for bringing them here is that of the victims and witnesses unit. They look after them; they pay for them and they return them. Perhaps all you do is to give them the list of the witnesses who would be appearing for the week and then they will try and do that. I expect you will do that because that is the only way we could move smoothly. If you looked at your list of witnesses, even your updated one, you will also find that you can easily adjust and get some of these witnesses much quicker than you have done before. To project for five witnesses who are likely to say about the same thing and thinking that irrelevancies might be ignored makes it difficult for one to be efficient and effective. From my observation, you have to provide for not less than ten witnesses every week. If we do not exhaust them, there can be a normal overflow and they will join the next week and we will see. But definitely that depends on the need to call the witnesses themselves because that is what creates a lot of problems. We will now give the appropriate directive for the witnesses you are likely to call so that we make sure that the administration cooperates with you when you ask for the increase.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, have I understood you well that you give me permission to call these two witnesses, even though they were not announced on the list for this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can call them. There's no problem. We still have tomorrow and Friday to sit. I hear we have no sitting on Monday but we will continue on Tuesday. At that time, your other witnesses for next week have arrived, and I think you should be able to supplement even that one so that we will take all of them next week. You have permission to request them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The Prosecution's position on this is that we're anxious to cooperate as much as we can in moving along the calling of witnesses. The only thing we ask is that we're given the names of these witnesses preferably before lunch today or by lunchtime today so that we can prepare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you can cooperate by giving the names of the witnesses to the Prosecution so they can prepare.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will know by noon whether they will be able to come in fact. I think they will and then we will immediately inform the Prosecution and my colleagues on the Defence of their names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: But in addition to that, those who are likely to arrive, those witnesses for next week who are likely to arrive, we can start with them on Friday because I hear you are expecting witnesses tomorrow to arrive by the victims and witnesses unit. When they do arrive, we can start with them on Friday instead of having another unmerited holiday. You can now call the witness. Call the witness, please. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please swear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may sit down, please. SADIK DZUMHUR

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for not having informed you yesterday that there was a possibility of you being called, so it's an apology to you and also to the Trial Chamber because you were not in your hotel room, otherwise we could have started with your testimony yesterday. Will you please introduce yourself to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Sadik Dzumhur.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I proceed with my questions, I wish to draw your attention to a technical matter. Actually, my questions and your answers need to be understood by everyone in the courtroom. For that purpose, the interpreters need time to translate both the questions and the answers. You will hear on the headphones, on the table, the interpretation of my question, and only then will you please answer that question; is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, will you please tell me when and where you were born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Konjic in 1945 on the 6th of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the court what is your educational background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I completed the highest school of administration in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is your citizenship, Mr. Dzumhur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My citizenship is Bosniak, a citizen of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a legal officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Dzumhur, please, what position you held on the 6th of April, 1992 when the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think at the time, according to our war assignments, I was in the war presidency in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war in April, were you active in the defence forces of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did take part in certain combat operations. Earlier, I was administrator of the training centre attached to the TO staff in Konjic, so that I was given the assignment to allocate the republican war reserves which I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, at some point in time, were you transferred to the public security station in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was transferred to the public security station because, in view of my earlier experiences, I was requested to do that and to work in policing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For how long in 1992 did you remain in the public security station in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think until mid June in '92 when the preparations were underway for the Borci operation when, in fact, I left Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that as of mid June 1992 and later, you were mostly involved in combat operations together with units of the police or did you also engage in other activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, both. We participated in combat in Glavaticevo when a unit of the MUP was subordinated to the municipal staff and our task was to go to Glavaticevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, is it true that upon arrival in The Hague, you handed over to me some personal documents indicating what your duties were in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I did hand over those documents to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May I ask for the usher's assistance to show Mr. Dzumhur these documents confirming the testimony of this witness regarding his activities and duties. Can the document be marked for identification, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence document 179/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, is this your personal document which you received as a member of the special unit of the public security station in Konjic when you were engaged in security of the war presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was issued by Mr. Guska, chief of the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since this is a document belonging to this witness, confirming his duties in a particular period of time, I'm tendering it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The document is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true to say, Mr. Dzumhur, that also upon arrival in The Hague you gave a representative of the Defence your official identity document which has an indication of your authority as a member of the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should also like to ask for the usher's assistance to show the witness this document and for it to be marked for identification first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence document 180/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, is this your own official identity card as a member of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are the authorisations of the holder of this identity card indicated in this card?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As this is a document belonging to this witness, indicating the authorisations of this witness, in support of the credibility of this witness, and which is relevant to this case because it shows the responsibilities of a part of the armed forces, I am tendering it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have already said something about this, and could you now tell us regarding your war assignment, in the month of April, within the war presidency, which task were you involved with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was involved in police matters providing security to the war presidency and, as I have already told you, I was an administrator in the training centre. I had some experience in that regard so that was the kind of assignment that I received.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a member of the public security station in Konjic, do you know whether, after the adoption of new regulations in mid April, your chief of the MUP was a member of the war presidency of the municipality of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was a member of the war presidency. However, he was not a subordinate to the war presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us who he was subordinate to, who the chief of the public security station was subordinate to, that is, the MUP in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The public security station of Konjic was subordinate directly to the republic MUP, to the ministry of the interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was MUP, according to the regulations of Bosnia and Herzegovina and according to the practise at that time, was it part of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, the court already knows, from certain evidence that has been heard here, that persons of Serb nationality from the area of the Town of Konjic were arming themselves illegally before the war through the assistance of their party, the SDS. Could you tell us if the public security station in Konjic had any orders from its ministry and any authority, any authorisation, to search for such weapons, to detain such persons and to conduct interrogations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to our regulations, carrying firearms was illegal. The public security station had authority to detain persons who violated, who violate such regulations. They also have the authority to interrogate them and to seize such weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since an immediate threat of war was declared in the country, could you tell us if you, yourself, during that time, if you -- if from the ministry of the interior, you received an order to intensify your activities regarding a search of persons who were illegally armed and regarding the seizure of such weapons and detention of these persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, such an order was received by everyone in the public security station and we did increase, intensify our activities. We had a number of cases like that, a number of reports indicating that persons of Serb nationality were illegally arming themselves. This was happening in the town itself and the countryside and the surrounding villages, so we organised a number of actions and we managed to collect a certain amount of weapons. I was personally involved in a number of these actions and if you want me, I can tell you specific example. We found a rifle, M-48 in one of the flats, a 7.9 calibre, it was under an aquarium, it was fully charged with five bullets.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, are you aware of any such searches being conducted in the area of the villages, Celebici and Idbar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had drafted a plan of action, including Celebici and Idbar and unit of Rale Musinovic received an assignment in that regard. They were supposed to uncover the perpetrators, detain them and seize their weapons. This happened and I believe that the detention place was the barracks in Celebici. At the time we didn't dispose of any other such premises.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, do you remember when the barracks of Celebici was first used for detention and interrogation of persons who were found to be in possession of firearms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have already told that. I think that this happened in Celebici and Idbar during the action of seizure and location of such persons. I think that was the first time that these people were arrested and taken to Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us if this was before the combat activities in Donje Selo and Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Bradina, that is, in Donje Selo, we had received a report.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to go into that right now. Could you tell us about Rale Musinovic and the searches in Celebici and the detention of these people. Did that occur in May, before these police and military operations took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, do you know Mr. Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know Zejnil Delalic before the war, I knew him only because people were talking about him, they respected him and I heard that he had bought some equipment, some very expensive equipment for -- dialysis in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know, were you personally introduced to Mr. Zejnil Delalic at the beginning of war, did you know that he was in Konjic at that time and did you meet with him at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, I didn't meet with him except for maybe one or two occasions in the war presidency. He was together with Saban Duracic who had a task to prepare the premises of the war presidency which was supposed to be transformed into a local centre, cultural centre and they were discussing some practical arrangements in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, we have heard here, the president of the war presidency, but in view of your assignments within the war presidency, do you have any personal knowledge as to whether Zejnil Delalic was a member of war presidency at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was not a member of the war presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, since the court is also aware that in the territory of the Municipality of Konjic, there is a number of military facilities, could you now tell us whether you know which military facilities were taken over in the month of April and were you, in any way, involved in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that I heard at the time that the barracks in Celebici were supposed to be surrendered without any fighting. That had apparently had been agreed upon. And one member of policemen was drafted into a team and there was also one unit from the Territorial Defence which took part in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But were you personally involved, a member of that group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not personally involved, but I had a task to receive the weapons at the farm of Mr. Zejnil Delalic, that is the farm of his sister, which farm was taken for the needs of the municipal staff at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, if you know, who brought the weapons to the farm and who, in addition to yourself, took over the weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Major Kevric who took over the weapons together with me, and the weapons were brought by Zejnil Delalic and some other people from the Territorial Defence. I think they brought the weapons in a Lorry, a FAP Lorry, a yellow Lorry, as far as I can remember. And part of the weapons was immediately distributed to the combat fighters who had no weapons, who were unarmed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were any other military actions regarding the take-over of the JNA facilities in Konjic at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These actions were mostly a mixture of police and military actions. I remember there was a very heavy shelling at that time by the former JNA after the take-over of the facility. They had dropped several bombs, each weighing 500 kilograms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move to another issue. The court also knows that the Town of Konjic was encircled and surrounded and that communication lines had been cut-off at the beginning of May. Could you tell us now what kind of connections, what links did the MUP have with the surrounding area, especially Sarajevo, and in what way did that communication function? How did they contact their subordinate ministry -- superior ministry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had its centre for communications, from time to time we would use the communication centre of the Territorial Defence, which was located in the family house of Mr. Zejnil Delalic. And it was good equipment, so from time to time we would use it, but not very often.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, do you know what happened with the Celebici barracks after it had been taken over from the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several units, one of the units from the MUP, headed by Rale Musinovic took over the barracks. They took up their quarters there and they remained there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, do you know when the operation for the lifting of the blockade of Donje Selo was conducted and what kind of role did the public security station, that is the MUP in Konjic have, the units to which you belong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were trying the resolve the problem through negotiations. The then commander of the police and myself, upon a verbal order of the chief, we went to Celebici and we tried to tell them that they should surrender the weapons peacefully and that the extremes should be removed so that a normal life would continue. They did not agree to that and they threatened us with liquidation. One part of the police force, which was not sufficient at the time, because we had information that they were heavily armed was there and we then requested assistance from the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who signed the order for lifting of the blockade of Donje Selo, did you see personally that order and do you know who it was signed by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know who signed the order. On behalf of the Territorial Defence, it was Mr. Ahmed Boric who signed the order and on behalf of the HVO, it was Dinko Zebic and also Jasmin Guska, who, at the time, was the chief of the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During that military operation, Mr. Dzumhur, were there any casualties, was anyone killed from the defence forces of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes, two policemen were killed during that operation, Boric and Niksic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Dzumhur, whether during that operation, a number of inhabitants of Donje Selo was arrested, that is persons who had taken part in the military operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certain people were arrested. They -- most of them surrendered to the military police of the HVO, they thought it was some kind of -- they would be safe in that way. However, certain numbers surrendered to the MUP units and they were all taken to Celebici after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, do you know anything about the fighting in Bradina and possible arrest and detention of people after that operation? To put more precisely, do you know anything specific about the operations and who was in charge of arresting and detaining people who were captured during that operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On several occasions, my chief and myself, we visited the area and these people, the people, the rebels who were surrendering, who surrendered, were then handed over to the military police of the HVO and the Konjic MUP. And they were taken to Celebici by buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, at that time, before the war and at the beginning of the war, and during these military operations, was there a prison in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a prison in Konjic, but it was used exclusively for the needs of the MUP. It consisted of three cells, I believe, and this was by no means enough. Yes, this was not enough for all of these persons who had been detained and that's why the chief of the station, Jasmin Guska, probably in consultations with some representatives of the HVO, decided that the place -- the detention place would be in Celebici, because, at the time, the Celebici facility was not shelled, it was situated far enough from the military operations. It was possible to improvise something there and it was a suitable place and that's why they decided to use it for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, is this something that you know personally, from your personal knowledge, were you present when your chief issued such an order to the members of the MUP, who were arresting these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was personally present there. We had already been told about that. Members of the MUP and the HVO were already informed about that and I was also personally told by the chief that that would be the most suitable way of handling the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, do you know if any weapons were found in the possession of these people, the people who were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were found in possession of weapons and persons who surrendered, they had probably discarded their weapons beforehand, so in accordance with that, in view of such a situation, we had previously been ordered to search the area. The action lasted for about one month and throughout that period, we managed -- we found about 700 pieces of weapons, rifles, machine guns, a certain amount of ammunition, hand grenades and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, do you know what happened with the people who were arrested at that time? Was it necessary at that time to conduct interrogations of these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After they were accommodated in the facility, an investigation committee was established. And as far as I can remember, I think that certain members of the MUP and members of the HVO and I don't know whether there was one member of the TO. Anyway, these were the people who composed this -- who were members of this commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the president of the commission was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know. It was Goran Lokas, who, at that time, was chief of security at the joint command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You indicated that there was a number of inspectors, detectives from the MUP who were members of this commission, do you know, Mr. Dzumhur, who appointed these people to the investigation commission, the commission that was supposed to conduct investigation against the arrested persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that Jasmin Guska was the representative of the MUP at that time and that he was the one who appointed certain members. The HVO also appointed a number of people to the commission -- of Croatian nationality and there was one more person, I believe that his name was Pajic, Detective Pajic, and he was appointed by the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have told us something about military operations in Donje Selo and Bradina. Could you now tell us, do you know whether Zejnil Delalic, according to your personal knowledge, took part in any of these operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the end of May, 1992, did you learn at one point that Zejnil Delalic was appointed coordinator by the war presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is something I heard at the time. It was a very important event for the presidency, Mr. Delalic was an important person, a businessman and who was the only person who was able, at the time, to hold such a post.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before I ask you one other question, I would like to know whether the MUP was a part, whether it belonged to the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it did, but it was not subordinate, it was not under the command of the joint command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Dzumhur, whether Zejnil Delalic, since he was coordinating the work between the defence forces and the war presidency, and as you just pointed out, the MUP was not within the joint command, do you know if he ever contacted with the representatives of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know, he had several contacts with the chief of MUP in connection with certain logistic problems. The MUP had remained almost intact in terms of equipment and weapons. They had the weapons that the joint command did not have, so they probably discussed the possibility of distribution of these weapons, especially in -- during the actions in which MUP was not taking part.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a coordinator, was Zejnil Delalic in any way, any time superior, in superior position in relation to the public security station and you, yourself, personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he wasn't, and he could not be superior in any way to them because it was the responsibility, the authority of the ministry of the interior of the republic and he could not be, he was not a superior to any of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have just stated who was in charge of the appointment of the members of the investigative commission and you know who was personally involved in that within the MUP, could you now tell us whether at that time, according to your personal information, Zejnil Delalic was involved in the appointment of the members of the investigative commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you that the military investigative commission consisted of members of the MUP, representatives of the HVO and one person from the Territorial Defence. Zejnil Delalic, therefore, had no authority or competencies to appoint anyone to that commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, who appointed Croats, members of the HVO, to the commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, all HVO members were appointed by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that Goran Lokas was appointed president of this military investigative commission. Mr. Dzumhur, do you know whether Mr. Lokas, at the beginning of June, 1992, whether he left Konjic at one point in time or whether he ceased working in that commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that he remained within the commission for about 10 days and then he had some traffic accident and he had problems with his knee and that was the reason why he stopped working for the commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if anyone from the HVO, after that, took over and whether anyone from the HVO continued working for the military investigative commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, because this particular post belonged to the HVO and it was Mr. Jerko Kostic who was delegated to that post, from the HVO in Mostar, as a replacement for Lokas.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, did you know Jerko Kostic from before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: According to your understanding of the function that Mr. Delalic had at the time as a coordinator and as the person in charge of logistics, was he the person who was able to appoint Mr. Kostic to any post, any function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not possible. I have already stated that it was the exclusive authority of the HVO to appoint members of the Croatian nationality of the HVO to that commission. And Mr. Kostic could only be appointed by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, did the public security station give any authority over the military investigative commission or over any other kind of action in connection with the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it could not do such a thing. It would have been illegal.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, while you were carrying out your duties as a member of the public security station, were you ever in the possession of some information as to the results of the interrogation conducted by the representatives of the military investigative commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not. However, the people who were interrogated at the time had been armed, that was proved. And we sent several patrols out in the field on the basis of what they had told the commission, on the basis of the information that they had provided us with.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, were you at any point in time informed, in writing or orally, about the work of the investigative commission or about the interrogations of the arrested persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the public security station or you, yourself, received any report regarding alleged mistreatment of the arrested persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I haven't received any such document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, you have indicated that Mr. Zejnil Delalic never received any authority from the public security station in connection with this investigative commission. From your personal knowledge, could you tell us whether Zejnil Delalic had any authority, any competencies to release or to detain such persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He never had such authority. He was not able to detain anyone. Such a possibility simply did not exist at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, do you know that at the beginning of the work of the commission, a certain number of persons were released and do you know what kind of response such decisions of the military investigative commission received from others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that between 50 and 60 people were released at the very beginning by the commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know, at the time, that certain persons had authority to release prisoners, regardless of the commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that the chief of the public security station, Jasmin Guska, on one occasion released a person by the name of Zelenovic from Bradina; however, the person by the name of Kovacevic from Konjic, Smajo Kovacevic, who reacted. He, I think, had asked the chief to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, do you know that the military investigative commission ceased to function at one point in time? If you know that, are you aware of any reasons why they stopped working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they had probably completed their work or maybe they were given other assignments. I don't know anything else about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since we have discussed the manner in which these persons were released, I would now like to know, Mr. Dzumhur, whether you, at any point in time in any way, were involved, whether directly or indirectly, in the release of any detained person from Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In an indirect manner, yes, I was involved. I think the name of the person was Golubovic. After the killing of the two policemen in Donje Selo, Golubovic was a suspect because he had a sniper rifle, but he and his father were very good hunters and they had very good rifles. So he was a suspect for the killing of these two policemen. I heard certain rumours from my colleagues. There was an anti-Serb atmosphere in Konjic at that time and we had to work hard to quell passions. In the area of Tisovac, Chetniks were conducting some operations, and I said to one of my colleagues that there were lots of fools who were likely to enter Celebici and to do something which would cause us a lot of trouble later on, something that would influence a number of subsequent events, so I tried to do something about that. While we were discussing, he made a contact with Cerovac who, at that time, was replacing Commander Ramic and he mentioned to him this problem. I don't know what happened later on, but I know that this person by the name of Golubovic was subsequently released.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, you were saying that after the take-over of the barracks, a unit headed by Rale Musinovic was accommodated there. Will you tell us, please, upon whose orders or who could have issued orders for this MUP unit to be stationed there and to interrogate the detainees in the Celebici barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This order was issued by the chief of the public security station, Jasmin Guska, and he was the only person who could have done it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During the time that Rale Musinovic was engaged in these activities, who was he subordinated to or, rather, who was his superior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His superior was the chief, Jasmin Guska.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that Zejnil Delalic at the time engaged in logistics and was a coordinator between the war presidency and the defence forces. Could he have in any way been a superior to Rale Musinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He could not have been his superior in any sense of the word because I said a number of times that Rale Musinovic belonged to the public security station and that his superior was the chief of that station, Mr. Jasmin Guska.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Dzumhur, whether, at the time, there were members of any other police within the Celebici compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a unit of the HVO military police. I think that heading that unit was somebody called Ivica Vujicevic or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the commanding officer of that military police unit of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It must have been the leader of the unit who was again subordinated to the HVO commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, according to your personal knowledge and understanding of the role played by Mr. Delalic at the time, could he have been a superior to Ivica Vujicevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the chain of command is clear. The superior to Vujicevic was the military police leader who was, again, accountable to the HVO commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, do you know until what date members of the MUP and the HVO military police provided security for the barracks and security for the detention centre that existed in Celebici at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They performed those duties until the end of June, when I left to another assignment, that is, the Borci Operation. From then on, I did not go back to Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that, at the very beginning of the war, you were active in the Territorial Defence staff, and I understood that you were aware that a joint command was formed. On the basis of your general knowledge or personal experience, do you know who the guards were accountable to? If you don't know, you will tell us so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that all the guards there, after TO units arrived there, were subordinate to the municipal TO staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, please tell me, are you aware, as a member of the MUP, whether at any point in time in 1992, the detainees in the Celebici prison were used to do work, cleaning work in town or something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were never used. I apologise for smiling because they couldn't have been used as the town was exposed to constant shelling. I think only occasionally they were used to clean the compound, which was in their own benefit, or maybe to repair a car or something.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, you also said that occasionally, as the public security station, you also used the communication centre of the Territorial Defence housed in the ground floor of Mr. Zejnil Delalic's house. Why did you use that communication centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, our own communication centre, as compared to the TO communication centre, was far inferior. So we went to the municipal staff's communication centre which, as I said, was housed in Mr. Zejnil Delalic's house. Those were the reasons, and we used that centre occasionally because of its power. It was a powerful centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me go on to another area now. Mr. Dzumhur, you said that one of your units took part in the Oganj Operation in the direction of Glavaticevo. As a part of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you and under what circumstances second or transfer your units to another command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this did occur and we did so in two ways, either by transferring units to another command or by organising joint actions. On a number of occasions, we would transfer some TO units to another command, depending on the needs of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the Operation Oganj, the aim of which was to liberate the area in Borci, do you remember whether your unit in that operation was under the command of the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was and I remember that was one of our most difficult tasks that we had, and I remember this because my son was with me in that operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you recall if, sometime in 1992, Zejnil Delalic became a military commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent quite some time on Mount Igman after that. Sometime, I think in the beginning of August, I heard that Zejnil Delalic had been designated as head of a group to make a breakthrough towards Sarajevo. I was heading a unit of the MUP forces which was then subordinated to Tactical Group 2, and our goal was the same, to make a breakthrough to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time Zejnil Delalic was commander of that group, did any of the units of the Konjic MUP come under his command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was any unit, in a previous or later period, belonging to the Konjic MUP, come under the command of one of the commanders of Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mentioned that it was, I think, subordinated to Polutak. I think it was one unit. This was to do with Hadzici, Tinovo Brdo and something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When a unit is transferred to the command of another commander, be it Polutak or Commander Alic, is all the authority transferred to the commander of the Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for as long as the operation lasts, but upon return to base, all authority ceases.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: While that unit is under the command of the commander of Tactical Group, either, 1 or 2, did other units of the public security station remain in Konjic? If they did, under whose command were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The units, of course, remain and they are always under the command of the same person, that is, the chief of the public security station, Jasmin Guska.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, after becoming commander of Tactical Group 1, was Zejnil Delalic at any point in time the commander of all formations of the public security station of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: According to your knowledge, as a commander of Tactical Group 1, was Zejnil Delalic, at any point in time, a commander over all the units of the HVO in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's nobody's case that he was ever the commander of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, General Divjak told you that all formations of the armed forces implied the HVO, MUP and the TO, and that that appointment has no sense because all formations cannot be all formations. That is why I'm asking this witness, who lived in Konjic, whether he can confirm what General Divjak testified to in this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You should ask that question from an HVO man. He's a MUP man. He can only talk about his own department.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, he comes from Konjic and he's familiar with far more details than we are.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you know this about Mr. Zejnil Delalic, as commander of Tactical Group 1, can you tell us, according to your personal knowledge, where was Tactical Group 1 based?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think at first in Pasaric and then on Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a citizen of Konjic and as a person employed in the public security station, do you know whether the base of the Tactical Group, the headquarters of the Tactical Group, was transferred from Pasaric to the house of Mr. Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know for sure that it was not because something like that is not logical. People could not come from Mount Igman to Konjic. The distance is 40 kilometres and more between the two. These areas were under shelling so it was not possible to travel always. The headquarters were stationed next to the units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After the appointment of Mr. Zejnil Delalic as commander of Tactical Group 1 and after he went to the area of combat, did you come across him personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge or did anyone ever tell that you Zejnil Delalic had any responsibility over the Celebici prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never heard anything to that effect, that Zejnil had any responsibility. This is the first time I hear any such things.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear or do you know yourself whether any of the guards from the Celebici prison were members of Tactical Group 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, two more questions only. Do you know that sometime in 1992, a smear campaign was launched against Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when Zejnil Delalic left Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that, after he left this campaign against him as a member of the intelligence service was intensified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was intensified. All kinds of rumours were spread about him. And those of us living there who knew that all of this was nonsense, we just laughed at this propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dzumhur. That ends my examination-in-chief of this witness, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examination from the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let's hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, while he's going to the microphone, I have an 11.30 meeting the registry has asked me to attend. Will the court excuse me for a few minutes and I may be a few minutes late returning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I will have a few questions on cross-examination. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Sir, my name is Tomislav Kuzmanovic and I represent Mr. Mucic in this case. There are several questions I'd like to ask you. Along those lines, if you don't know the answer, an "I don't know" is sufficient. We don't want you to guess, okay? Do you understand? You have to answer "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. I said "yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear you, I'm sorry. If the answer can be given as a "yes" or a "no," that will be sufficient as well; do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are aware, sir, that on June 11th of 1992, there was an order which ordered the MUP guards within the sports centre Musala and Celebici to be cancelled and that TO guards numbering 20 to 30 people where the security of the prison should be formed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that on June 11th of 1992 this proposal that I discussed earlier of the switching of the guards, that guards would be taken from the structure of the Konjic second unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that because I told you earlier on that in mid June, I was engaged in other activities relating to preparations for Operation Borci.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "mid June," do you have a specific date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The exact date for what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That you were involved in other activities outside of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, this happened six or seven years ago so it is impossible to remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did those duties take you, sir, outside of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my testimony, I said that one of our units was transferred under the command of the TO in Operation Borci and the actual location was Zljebine next to Glavaticevo. These were our initial positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Did that take you outside of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The answer that he did not know is sufficient. I think if he was not around he could not have known.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I'm telling you it's improper to ask such questions. He said he didn't know, he wasn't around and he was not in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: After mid June of 1992, you had essentially nothing to do with what was going on in Konjic; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had nothing to do with some things, and some other things I had something to do with, like police affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Why don't you describe for us, sir, what things you did have to do with after mid June 1992 in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had to do with people working in logistics in the MUP to provide certain materiel so that we could prepare for Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it a fair statement, sir, that after mid June 1992, you had no personal knowledge of anything that may have been going on inside of Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you have an idea of the distance between Celebici and Glavaticevo, and at the time to go to Glavaticevo, we had to cover about 150 to 200 kilometres across Mount Igman and the villages at the foot of Mount Bjelasnica. Anyway, I wasn't really interested as to what was happening in Celebici. There were people who had those responsibilities. I had others and I was focusing on those.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that, sir. A simple "yes" or "no" would have sufficed. Is it a fair statement that after mid June 1992, you did not receive any written orders that were related to Celebici at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not receive any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But you haven't asked him if he received any written orders with regard to Celebici before June. Ask him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That was my next question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Had you received any written orders before mid June 1992 in regard to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If such orders had been issued, who in your organisation would be the one to receive these orders?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Tell him what sort of orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Orders relating to Celebici. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But that is a wide field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It is a wide field. If he knows, I'll narrow it down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Please narrow it down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, I said that a commission was formed in Celebici, and the members of that commission had a joint body and they reported to the people who had appointed them. They couldn't submit to me any reports, nor did I receive any reports. They would report to the people who were their superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, should we break here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Have you any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will have some further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will break now and reassemble at 12 noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please kindly invite the witness. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I just have a couple more questions for you. I would like to have a couple of documents marked for identification with the assistance of the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please identify them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence document D-10/2 and D-11/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May the Prosecution know of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am sorry, I have a copy for the Prosecution. I don't have a copy of the second one and I apologise, but if you would like to have a look at it before the witness does, that would be fine with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Excuse me, is there any translation into English of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, there's not, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: How could you tender them?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will provide the translation after the break, if that is all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What is this document about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it’s an order relating to the setting up of the investigatory commission and also the report of the investigatory commission. I apologise for not having them translated for everyone here. If Your Honours would like, I could make sure that it gets translated over the lunch hour and they could be admitted subject to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may be of assistance, my colleague has recently joined us. As far as I can see from here, these documents have already been provided. Can I please have a look at them? Maybe some of them have already been admitted into evidence. Yes, this document, for example, the 15th of June, is part of the expert opinion of the military expert. I cannot tell you what the exact number is, but it is the third volume, V5-D. There's also an English version of this text. If I may be of assistance, can I see the other document as well, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would ask for the assistance of the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are you sure this witness is in a position even to identify that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll find that out, Your Honour, when I ask him. That's document V/D -- I'm sorry, 5/D/18. Thank you, Counsel, and I apologise to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The other document, in order to facilitate things, as far as I can see, it is the document that has been admitted into evidence during the testimony of Witness D.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, rather than unnecessarily cluttering the case with more paper, I would ask that after the witness reviews documents that they be withdrawn with respect to their marking so that we don't have to have duplication and I apologise again for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, let's look at it and let's be sure whether he can identify it himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Whether he's in a position to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you want me to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like you to take a look at those documents, perhaps to refresh your recollection. Have you had a chance to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a report of the military investigative commission, which I never received, nor do I have anything to do with it. I can just read it and that's all. I have never had any such document in front of me and I am not familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Have you now --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have, Your Honour. Despite the fact that he's not seen them and not had them, I would like to ask him a few questions relating to events that relate to these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: A matter which he has no idea about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, he's reviewed the documents and I just want to ask him about specific dates of things relating to these documents. If Your Honour pleases, I will be very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am not too sure it's even right to do that because he says he's never read them, it was not sent to him, so he knew nothing about it, If he knew such a commission was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, he said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: And the composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That's all he knows about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if Your Honours will permit me, I will be very brief with respect to the questions I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you will note on the order, it's dated June 15th, correct, of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And the order, after you've read it, has to deal with the interrogation of persons regarding the military operation at Bradina, is that correct, at least according to what the order says?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, please ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The copies of who was supposed to get the order, as far as the document is concerned, don't include anyone who would be, at least at June 15th of 1992, associated with running or commanding Celebici?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I believe that these are matters on the face of the document, you can understand it to be so. If it is so indicated on the face of the document, you don't have to ask him about it unless he's never received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: With respect to the second document, sir, which is the report, that's also dated June 18th, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And that confirms that at least as far as the people who are listed on that report all had weapons on them, correct, from your recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have never read this document and I never had the need for such a document. I never saw it. It was not directed to me, and here it says, "Military Investigative Commission" without any signatures or any other such markings. So a report like this should contain, in my opinion, all necessary information. It should have the marking "military secret" on that and so forth. I have never seen such a document. It was not possible that I would be the addressee of such a document and I cannot say anything about it. I cannot confirm it. I was not in charge of anything like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would ask that those documents be marked withdrawn, since they were marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I ask, for the record, that numbers of the exhibits be made clear because I think it doesn't come out clear enough in the record. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're taking a little while to get wired up and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first exhibit, D-10/2, is the document identical to the Defence Exhibit, Annex 5-D, 18/1. And Defence Exhibit D-11/2 is identical to Prosecution Exhibit 162.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: And counsel applied to withdraw those exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: They have not been tendered but they have been marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, as well, they should be.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, but this is not the evidence that has been just read out, D-162, this is a completely different piece of evidence. This is a Defence Exhibit that was introduced through Witness D. The evidence that has just been read by the registry refers to the information regarding the prison in Celebici and we are talking about the Defence Exhibit here, D-50/1. This is an abbreviated version of the report on the arming of the population of Serb nationality in Brdani, dated 18th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. You Honour, I want to say, I appreciate you allowing me to leave a few minutes early for a meeting which turned out to be cancelled and I apologise. Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: My name is Tom Moran and I am going to be asking you a few questions. Most of my questions probably just call for a "yes" or "no" answer. If you listen to my questions and if you don't understand them, will you stop me and I'll rephrase them and work with you so that you understand what I am asking? Will you do that for me, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I understand that you were present for some of the fighting at both Bradina and Donje Selo; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On several occasions, as I have already stated, I was part of the fighting, together with my chief, Jasmin Guska. I visited the area where the fighting was conducted, and later on also during the attack when Bradina fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let's focus on when Bradina fell. Was there any resistance from the people inside of the village or was it simply the troops of the government firing into the village and attacking without receiving resistance? I'll bet that question wasn't clear. Let me try that again. During the fighting, sir, did the people inside the village resist the government forces? For instance, was there a lot of firing from the village at the government forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You call it fighting. Do you mean by two people?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: One side doesn't fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, as you recall, there's been a lot of testimony here that there was no resistance from the village. This man was present there and I want to find out whether there was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What happened at the time they took over Bradina?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That should be enough for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: At that time, was there firing from the people inside the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I answer now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, let me clarify one thing that has to do with a war situation. When the road was deblocked, my colleague, Rajko Dordic, who was an operations manger of the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence, organised the deblocking of the road in accordance with the military regulations and strategies. He had dug out trenches and he did everything that was required in a military sense. He organised the blocking actually, I'm sorry. Then they entered the village and the firing started and it was a real war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So there was firing, a lot of firing from both sides at Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It happens all the time in a war. That's the way you do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I understand that, sir, and I just wanted to make it clear that both at Donje Selo and at Bradina there was fighting. As people on both sides were shooting at each other, there was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up to a certain point in time they did fire, but they realised that they were in such a situation that it would be stupid for them to get killed, and both sides understood that. It stopped and these persons started surrendering themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. By the way, both at Bradina and Donje Selo, we've heard testimony that there were some of the people fighting on the side of the Bosnian government, the government authorities. A group called the Green Berets, did you see any Green Berets fighting at either Bradina or Donje Selo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know only that Green Berets exist in Sarajevo. Such formations in Konjic, I am sure about that, never existed, nor do they exist now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, as I understand it, one of your duties after the fighting and after people were surrendering at both Bradina and Donje Selo was to arrange for their transport from Bradina and Donje Selo to the Celebici camp; is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to organise it, but to ensure a safe passage for the transport. It was not my task to provide vehicles and things like that and for them to enter the area. I was just supposed to provide a safe transport to Celebici because Konjic was exposed to constant shelling. I was in touch with them all the time and they kept informing me about the situation on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: As I understand it, at both Bradina and Donje Selo, prisoners were being loaded onto vehicles at several different locations at pretty much the same time; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, more or less, the way they kept coming, we transported them to the best of our possibilities at that time. We only disposed of several trucks and these were the vehicles that we used for transporting them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: As I understand it, while the loading was going on, you were moving pretty continually from place to place where people were being searched and loaded onto vehicles; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps not all the time, but I did visit these points. These checkpoints were not very far from the area. They were pretty close to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You didn't see the guards beating any prisoners, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My task, among other things, was also to make sure that such a thing does not happen, that prisoners do not get beaten, and I was successful to some extent in that. There may have been such cases, but that I didn't see. Perhaps they didn't do it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So if it happened, you didn't see it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now, after the prisoners were in Celebici, you visited the barracks several times, didn't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had been to the barracks several times before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I want to focus on the time period after the prisoners were in the barracks, when they were being housed in the barracks. You visited Celebici several times after that, didn't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You saw some of the prisoners while they were outside the hangar doing things; isn't that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were not many of them outside hangars. They were probably going to the toilet or something. There were not many of them, but that was all I simply saw, several people and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You didn't see anybody that looked like they had been beaten, had you? Did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I must tell you that all of us who had been involved in that, we all looked a little beaten up, you know, all of us at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Because of the fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because of various reasons and circumstances. If you were in Bradina, you probably saw the kinds of roads that we have. It's very difficult -- it's very likely that you can get injured and all kinds of injuries happened at that time, fractures, falls and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Of course during the fighting with people running through the woods and things like that, they're going to pick up scratches and injuries of all sorts, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I, myself, tripped several times. I mean, you can see the traces on my face.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, when the people were arrested at Celebici -- excuse me, at Bradina and Donje Selo, did you just simply arrest everybody you could find or did you arrest just people that you had reason to believe had been armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, let me clarify. I never arrested anyone. This was done by the MUP units and the military police of the HVO, but in most of the cases, people would surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And many of them surrendered with their arms, with their weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that. They surrendered to the police of the HVO, but it's true that we found lots of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: By the way, and this is going to sound like a silly question, but at the time in May and June of 1992, it was illegal in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina for citizens to have military type weapons, machine guns, hand grenades, fully automatic rifles, that kind of thing; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was a criminal offence according to our laws. It was illegal to possess military weapons and military equipment, something that would be used in military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, I thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may it please the court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Sir, I just have one question, and I am defence attorney for Esad Landzo, Cynthia McMurrey. You are aware of the murder of a group of military police in the middle of July of 1992; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learned about it immediately after the killing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: In fact, you appeared on the scene of the murder; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, immediately after the murder.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That was an extremely brutal murder of about nine military police; would that be accurate to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's an excellent description. That is exactly what it was; it was brutal. One of them had his ears cut off. That is how the Chetniks acted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: As a result of this murder, it caused a general outrage and anger in most of the population of the Konjic municipality against the Serbs, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it wasn't a generalised feeling, but it significantly increased tensions in the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, thank you very much.
