utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any questions by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir, my name is Turone and I am going to ask you some questions for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You said this morning something about the investigating commission headed by Goran Lokas and you said something about Mr. Delalic concerning this commission. You said he didn't have any function for appointing members, if I am not wrong. My question is: Did Mr. Delalic have any other function whatsoever, anyhow related to the investigating commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my testimony, you were able to see that he had no function there because he was a civilian and because he was a coordinator. If I need to clarify what --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary, thank you. You said just a few minutes ago that you visited Celebici several times after the prisoners were brought there. Can you say approximately how many times did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know for sure but three or four times with the chief of public security, Jasmin Guska, and I was present there maybe twice when he personally questioned some prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was that the purpose of your visits? Which was the reason for your visits there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The purpose of our visit was a routine tour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, isn't that true that on 31 May, '92 in the courtyard of the MUP building in Konjic, you were present when a group of Serb prisoners, including among others Rajko Dordic and Novica Dordic were heavily beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that they were never brought in front of the MUP building and I met Mr. Dordic in the MUP but not then and with that group, and I brought him pills because Mr. Dordic worked with me and I knew that he suffered from kidney trouble and had difficulties with his eyes and I brought him these pills and that is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So if a witness testified about these facts I told you, in this same courtroom, and said that you and other MUP leaders watched the beating without reacting to it, that testimony would be incorrect; is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I claim, and I'm under oath, that there was never any beating of Mr. Dordic in my presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: If the witness came in this courtroom --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: -- And said that you were there and watched the beating without reacting to it. You say that this testimony would not be correct; is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that Rajko Dordic was never beaten up in front of the MUP in my presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I understand that. My question was about if a witness said something different about this and said that you and other MUP leaders watched this beating of members of Serb people, including Rajko Dordic and Novica Dordic, you mean that this testimony is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I'll take his answer that it is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He said it twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Dzumhur, isn't it true that in the first half of June, in an area inside Celebici, close to tunnel 9, you were present when a group of Serb prisoners, including among others Zara Mrkajic and Miro Golubovic were heavily beaten by Bato Alkadzic and other soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At what time was this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to tell you the time. Please answer my question. Isn't that true that in the first half of June, before mid June approximately, one day during that period of time in an area of Celebici close to Tunnel 9, you were present there when a group of Serb prisoners, including Zara Mrkajic and Miro Golubovic were heavily beaten by guards and soldiers and Bato Alkadzic was one of them; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe I visited Celebici for the last time in June, but that was at 12.00 at night. We came on a routine control and I never was present at any such event. We came about midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was there any time you were present in Celebici when prisoners were beaten and you could see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Sir, I worked professionally in the army. I know the code of conduct. I'm familiar with the Geneva Conventions and I know what I had to do and that is how I acted. I didn't spend any time there. If I did have to go to Celebici, I came to do my work, my police work, and left. In other words, I was doing my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you. This is my last question. If another witness testified about these beatings inside Celebici in that circumstance and did that in this courtroom, and if this witness said that you and other MUP leaders were present right there and did not prevent the beating from taking place, although seeing them, that testimony would not be correct, would it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me repeat. I'm under oath and I said that the last time I was in Celebici was about midnight and that I did not attend anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This concludes my cross-examination, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Let's get something clear. You went to the Celebici camp to the area used for holding the prisoners, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You were visiting the prison and the inmates when you went to Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said a moment ago, no, I didn't approach close, except a couple of times when the chief of police was interrogating a number of detainees, but I never entered the place where the prisoners were held, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You never went to the tunnel where many of them were held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you, by the way, know the person who was in charge of the prisons of Celebici? Who was the head at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What period of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Up to June 15 when, perhaps, you ceased to go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until June the 15th, I know that a MUP unit was accommodated in Celebici and that heading that unit was Rale Musinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: And you know that the MUP was in charge of the prisoners; they were looking after the persons detained there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that period, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When did they cease to take charge of the persons in the prisons there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I said about mid June new TO forces arrived and that several policemen remained behind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think this is all for this witness. Thank you for your assistance. You are discharged. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I said this morning, I have been in touch with our witnesses in Vienna and they have confirmed that they will be able to come here tomorrow by 12 noon, so that I could call the first of the two witnesses at 2.30. These are witnesses Ciso Ismet and Delalic Emir. Immediately during the recess, we will submit to the Trial Chamber, the Prosecution and our colleagues the names of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Actually, we have a few motions which have been submitted. I don't know to what extent counsel are prepared, but I wouldn't mind taking the motions at 2.30 when we resume. utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. I suppose we'll start with the motions in the way we have listed them here. The first one, I think, is a long standing one. The motion by Landzo, for adequate time to prepare defence, what do you say about that? Because you have adequate time. What is pressurising you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have to say that since I filed this motion, the registry and I have come to an agreement that they will bring an investigator to The Hague on June 10th to the 15th, so that complaint, I would like to waive. We still have a very significant problem. Considering the accelerated trial schedule that we're placed under right now, we all have expert witnesses and investigators that need to meet and consult with our clients and with the attorneys in order to prepare for the defence. What has occurred is, we're in trial Monday through Friday. The only time that any experts or investigators have to meet with the defendants themselves are after court, which is only from when they get back to the detention centre and would be from 6.30 to 8.30 or on the weekends. There are now in excess of 40 Defence lawyers involved in meeting with their clients at the detention centre. There are four rooms available and it's almost impossible to make the appointments in order to have sufficient time to meet with your client. We're asking that during the week, when we're in trial and the defendants are being held here in the Tribunal, I know it presents some kind of security problems, but I believe that the rights of the accused to a fair trial and adequate time to prepare their defence outweighs the security problems at this time. If during the breaks or during lunch period we could have the experts and the investigators utilise this down time here at the Tribunal, it would certainly assist everybody in time and preparation for their Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In this regard, have you spoken to the registrar? Maybe she can make some arrangements.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: We have spoken to the registry many times. I think everybody along this bench --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: On this particular problem?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What is their response?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Their response is that we only have a limited amount time. On Wednesday night it's even less than 8.30 to meet at the detention centre. And that's the Dutch regulations that we have to adhere to, since they're the host of the UN detention centre. Because the Dutch regulations don't allow for that, we are precluded from meeting with our clients then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Speaking for myself and not for any other person, I think you're familiar that it's a most unusual thing for a Defence, which has been known for more than a year before now, to start talking about this type of argument. Because I do not see -- I have read your motion and none of those issues is new. They have been with us, some of them been examined and you have indicated the possibility of these experts about some eight or nine months earlier than now, and you still talk about them. You think, even with this period, you are unable to get your expert to discuss with you and the accused. And the court should now wait and set perhaps a particular period for you to be ready. This is your argument. I don't know, it's never done in that way. Well, I have never known it to be done in that way. You may know it to be done in that way, but no need to be so. You've had sufficient time and the accused has been examined several times. You have even talked about these experts so many months before now, so I am not too impressed by all the arguments that you are putting forward. Also, your limitations and your ability to discuss these things and get it through, it doesn't impress me at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, I would like to state that I only became lead counsel recently and there was no preparation for the Defence prior that moment, except for my interviews when I went to Konjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You were on this trial since March last year.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I have, but, Your Honour, I was co-counsel and I didn't plan the strategy or develop the strategy of the Defence at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Anyway, it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Try to do your best. The trial is still on, you do your best.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am doing my best. I am doing my best, but all I was requesting was that we find some kind of arrangement to have more time to meet with the defendants outside of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That's not what the Trial Chamber can arrange because it's not within our power to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I filed this motion in March because that was the time Mr. Mucic had all his problems with the registry. And the Trial Chamber at that point said, don't let it get out of hand. If you have a problem that you can't solve with the registry, bring it to the court's attention. Therefore, that's what I did. And I was only abiding by what I thought was the proper procedure, according to what you said at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If it's an administrative matter, which we can give directions, we could do that. If it's a directive which might affect the regulations of the prisons and the way the Dutch authorities organise them, procedures, it's fairly difficult for us to break through.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: If it affects the rights of the accused, I believe it becomes a matter of the trial chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: So many things affect the rights of the accused and when they are competing rights, one has to give way.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I have one other issue that I would like to raise before the Trial Chamber in this motion. It's that, when Defence counsel go to Bosnia to do their investigation, we have to take cash, German Marks with us, out of our own pocket, to finance the trip ourselves. When we get there, we have to pay for our travel -- I mean, not our travel, our airline tickets are provided. We have to pay for our hotel room, we have to pay our investigator, we have to pay the rental car, we have to pay our interpreters. Frankly, we just can't afford to do that. We are asking that a quality of arms be had because the Prosecution does not have to come up with the money out of their pocket to finance their trips for investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I may just, actually, most of this is not the business of the Prosecution and so I don't want to do it, but it is the case that certain things, such as paying for the financial difficulties that may happen in trips, certainly have happened to the Prosecution too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Don't wait for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: We're equally in debt and paupers. I wish that there was some way that we could find a way to finance these investigative trips without having to go into debt, is my question. I have brought this up with the registry many times. Basically we would just like more access with our clients. Also, I would like it to be noted when our investigator goes to the prison to talk to the defendant, if the presence of the attorney is not -- if the attorney is not present, the meetings are not considered privileged and confidential. I think that that infringes upon our ability to prepare for a defence, that we have to present every time an investigator meets with the defendant. The confidentiality and the privileged information between the investigator and the defendant should be extended not only when the attorney is present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We have arrived to the general principle now, which is confidentiality between counsel and the accused. Now you want to extend it to include this investigator?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let me make a suggestion. Do you know how law is created? With time. Perhaps without pressing it for some time, the prison might understand. We'll try and explain to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: We'll work on that and try to get it privileged because our investigator is coming on June 10th and I would like to not have to be sitting there holding his hand when he meets with Mr. Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in connection with this proposal, although this does not concern the Defence of Zejnil Delalic in a direct way, I would just like to give my support to the endeavours of the Trial Chamber. We do need your support. At the moment we are presenting our case. Let me just point out to the fact that prison facilities are very small and it's very difficult for us to get enough time to meet with our clients. I am not going to say that we are doing this in a pantry or anything, but we are grateful for any room that we can have access to. There are 40 lawyers there, families also have the right to visit their relatives in the detention unit. Now that we are presenting our Defence in full manner, it is very difficult for us to get even one hour during the weekend to clarify certain things. That's why I would like to suggest, to the Trial Chamber, which has to ensure the rights of the accused, to make a proposal to the registry and this is what we've been doing, but the detention unit in a direct way, to give priority in according facilities and time at the detention unit, so that we are enabled, in this way, to work in an adequate manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You know, up to now, we had only one Trial Chamber. We now have about three or two, I would say, functioning. I suppose as time goes on and the facilities expand and the United Nations knows the pressures and everything, they'll do something. We're very cooped in our chambers and as time goes on, we'll cope with it more. Thank you. Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was going to suggest, we're guests of the Dutch facilities at the prison. We being the entire Tribunal family, if you would, and they're not going to change their rules for us, presumably. I know we have an investigator coming in, it will be the first time he's been in The Hague since before the trial, just to do final discussions with Mr. Delic. There's at least about three hours a day he could meet with him in this building. If it were permitted by the security people, that is something that the Tribunal controls. By the time someone gets to the Defence rooms, they've been through two metal detectors and are not likely to be smuggling any contraband or anything. In fact, our investigator is an attorney. We've not brought him in several times, frankly, because of the cost. If he's not meeting with Mr. Delic on a fairly regular basis, a vacation in The Hague, which I am sure he'll enjoy, but it would seem to be a waste of the United Nations' resources. We need these meetings just for the last minute preparation. We're planning tentatively, to having him talk to our colleagues. At about July the 6th, we're going to be putting on witnesses. So we need to get those final preparations and those final thoughts from Mr. Delic to the investigator directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Normally I come from a common law system where the judge is not informed with the accused regulation of his Defence. We're usually aloof and allow him to prepare his Defence and present it. I don't get involved with the accused's preparing his Defence and know who is doing it with him and those who are arranging it with him. Severely, doesn't concern -- one might speak to the authorities to assist him, but we are not participants in that type of arrangement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour and although we'd be more than grateful for any help. And I don't think you'd want to be meeting with your witnesses and helping prepare them, although we'd be most grateful for that. This is a technical thing and Ms. McMurrey has been the lead on this and at some kind of impasse. It's something that is really nobody's fault and nobody is pointing fingers of blame at anyone. When we started this trial, there were six people in the UN detention centre and now there's 26 and they have actually moved one into the regular Dutch facility outside of the UN facility just because it's so crowded. People have been arrested and people have been turning themselves in, and they are no longer fugitives from justice and that's a good thing. But all good things have their bad sides and at this point I think we're seeing the bad side that there has been such an increase in defendants, in such a short period of time, that no one has been able to cope with it and frankly, --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The length of the trial has also contributed to this condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would not disagree with you, I was counting it up and if you really want to know, I can compare the number of days Prosecution had with some other trials you've seen on television. I think we've been pretty prompt with this. Our trial has had problems again and they're no one's fault. You get an expert witness for the Prosecution that gets involved in a traffic accident in England, that's nothing any one can control and those things cause delays. But I don't think that any deliberate attempt on any one's part to delay this trial. I think everyone wants to get this trial done, and gone and over with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to briefly address the court on that same issue relating to more form related substance. But that form is very important. That's access to our client so we can adequately prepare our Defence. And as the case has been moving along, and as you know I am relatively new here. I have noticed that it is difficult to get quality time, so to speak, to be able to sit down, hash out the issues and go over the weeks testimony, go over whatever documents are necessary and to come to some conclusions. And along those lines are supportive of co-counsel's motion and perhaps plea that on the issue of form, that we be allowed some more meaningful access to our clients. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think that should be enough adequate time to prepare for the Defence. Now, the next one, I think we will join Defence presentation on request of evidence. Can we hear who is presenting that? Is it Ms. Residovic who is presenting that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have Michael Greaves who is a legal representative for all four defendants and we ask that the court allow leave of court to have Mr. Greaves argue this motion, on behalf of all of us, instead of the judicial economy, instead of hearing all four of us at a different time like you just did, you can hear from one person who represents all of us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We'll hear Mr. Greaves, we've missed him for some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. Your Honour, Articles 20 and 21 of the statute of this Tribunal can be given a short but, I hope, accurate label. These are the fair trial provisions that this Tribunal operates under. They are the kind of rules or provisions which are found in a number of different similar statutes throughout the civilised world. And, indeed, in one case before the appeals chamber in the Tadic case, the judges in that case noted that the fair trial guarantees that exist in Article 14 of the international covenant on civil and political rights have been adopted almost verbatim in Article 21 of our statute. They turn up in a number of different places in almost identical form, the European Convention on Human Rights or in national laws which are of the bill of rights type. They also appear in Article 75 of Protocol 1 of the Geneva Convention which has identical wording for those provisions which are made for persons who are detained and who are tried by the detaining power for war crimes. Those provisions, Your Honour, are set out in Articles 20 and 21. The relevant provisions are, in my submission on behalf of all four defendants, these: Article 20, paragraph 1, which require, because of the use of the words "shall ensure," that a trial is fair and expeditious, that the proceedings are conducted in accordance with the rules of procedure and evidence with full respect for the rights of the accused. What are those rights? In our submission, those rights are set out in Article 21 of the statute. It is headed "Rights of the Accused." The important ones in connection with this motion are these: Article 21(1) says that all persons shall be equal before the International Tribunal; 21(2), in the determination of charges against him, the accused shall be entitled to a fair and public hearing subject, of course, to Article 22, which is the victims and witnesses provision. Article 21(4), in the determination of any charge against the accused pursuant to the present statute, the accused shall be entitled to the following minimum guarantees in full equality, subparagraph (e) to examine or have examined the witnesses against him and to obtain the attendance and examination of witnesses on his behalf under the same conditions as witnesses against him. I stress those last seven words because, in our respectful submission, those are mandatory provisions which are not optional for this Tribunal, have to be applied, are mandatory.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask counsel to slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Looking at the generality of these provisions, they might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are being advised to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, thank you. They are what might properly be called the equality of arms provisions. Can I remind Your Honours of what the learned judge, Judge Vorah, said in his separate opinion on the Prosecution motion for production of Defence witness statements. That was in the case of Prosecutor versus Tadic, a decision rendered on the 27th of November, 1996. The learned judge said this concerning the equality of arms principle: "The principle is intended in an ordinary trial to ensure that the Defence has means to prepare and present its case equal to those available to the Prosecution which has all the advantages of the state on its side. The European Commission of Human Rights equates the principle of equality of arms with the right of the accused to have procedural equality with the Prosecution. It seems to me that from the above authorities that the application of the equality of arms principle, especially in criminal proceedings, should be inclined in favour of the Defence requiring parity for the Prosecution in the presentation of the Defence case before the court to preclude any injustice against the accused." I read that out in full because, in my respectful submission to Your Honours, that is a concise but accurate exposition of what all of us understand by the principle of equality of arms. Of course, no Defence counsel is going to say, "If the Prosecution have 20 investigators, we should have 20 investigators." That would be unrealistic, particularly as the duties of the Prosecution are much wider and greater than those of the Defence. But in a particular trial, equality of arms means the creation of a level playing field, so that the Prosecution operates according to the same regime as the Defence and vice versa. We respectfully submit that it is neither proper nor, indeed, lawful for different regimes as to the presentation of evidence to be applied as between the Prosecution and the Defence. That applies across the board, not just to the question of the calling of witnesses. As I've indicated, the provisions of Articles 20 and 21 are not optional but are mandatory guarantees to the Defence that they will be treated in precisely the same way as the Prosecution in respect of those matters which are set out as fair trial provisions. Can I remind Your Honours of this? During this case, the Prosecution were able to call such witnesses as they chose. There was one exception, as I recall, which led to the Prosecution applying to call a handwriting expert. That application was declined on very specific grounds and is not, in our submission, touched by the generality of the proposition that I've placed before you. Having called those witnesses, I think, and I'm sure Ms. McHenry will correct my mathematics if I'm wrong, 60 witnesses, the Prosecution were able to ask time and time again the same question. "What do you know of the murder of so and so? What do you know about the conditions pertaining in the camp," for example, questions which had been covered sometimes at great length by other Prosecution witnesses. At no stage did Your Honours seek to determine which witnesses the Prosecution could call, to pick and choose from their list or to establish a witness list of your own choosing which was different from that presented according to Your Honours' order by the Prosecution at the outset of the trial and amended from time to time. Rights the court does have are these: Under Rule 89, to exclude evidence which is irrelevant or has no probative value or should be excluded because of the provisions of 89(D), I think it is. Similarly, under Rule 95, you are entitled to exclude evidence on this basis: "No evidence shall be admissible if obtained by methods which cast substantial doubt on its reliability or if its admission is antithetical to and would seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings." We respectfully submit that there is no power in law under the rules or under the statute for Your Honours to choose on behalf of the Defence which witnesses the Defence calls. Your Honours will recall that shortly after the close of the Prosecution case and the determination of the submissions that were made at that time that there was no case to answer. The Prosecution submitted a motion which dealt with two matters; firstly, the point at which a defendant, if he chose to do so, could or should give evidence within his own defence case; secondly, the order in which cross-examination would take place of Defence witnesses as between the counsel of co-accused and the Prosecution. When dealing with the issue of the order in which Defence witnesses would be called, we submit that Your Honours applied the appropriate principle which is that it is not for Your Honours to organise and determine the Defence case. In our submission, the issue of the order in which witnesses are called is, in fact, a lesser one than the issue of which witnesses are called. If, as Your Honours determined, you have no right to determine at what point the defendant gives evidence, a fortiori we submit there is no power in Your Honours to determine which witnesses shall be called. If a witness is called who gives evidence which is irrelevant or which does not bear probative value, then, of course, Your Honours have extensive powers to say, "That evidence is irrelevant and will not be heard. That evidence is not of probative value and we will not admit it." But Your Honours do not have, we submit, under the rules, under the statute, the authority, the lawful power to determine on behalf of the Defence which witnesses will be called. The effect of what Your Honours seek to do is, in my submission, twofold. You seek to put yourselves, effectively, in the place of Defence counsel whose job it is to organise their defence and to decide and determine which witnesses are to be called. We respectfully submit that that is descending into the arena in a way which is not appropriate for a trial of this kind. Your Honour, in the motion or the response that the Defence made to the Prosecution's motion about the order of Defence witnesses, you may recall one example was given from the Belgian system. We submit that this is a sensible and accurate reflection of the fair trial provisions that exist throughout the civilised world. The quotation runs as follows and it comes from the International Encyclopaedia of Laws, Kluwer International. One of the most fundamental rules in Belgian evidentiary law is that an accused person is presumed to be innocent. That, of course, is our rule. This rule has several very important consequences as far as his legal position in this connection is concerned. The first one is that he is never obliged to prove his innocence. The second one is that he disposes of the privilege against self-incrimination, so nobody can compel him to cooperate in an active way in his own condemnation. The third one is implied in this privilege he has the right of silence. The fourth one is that if there is uncertainty about the proof of his guilt, he should be given the benefit of the doubt. This is the one that I wish to emphasise. The fifth consequence is that he is free to organise his Defence in the way that he wants. Your Honour, I say and make these submissions on behalf of all the defendants, not because one seeks to prevent Your Honours from chivvying people along, hurrying people up. Those are the tasks of all judges. I appear regularly in a court in North Hampton where we have a judge who regularly, sometimes to the great concern of those who have never appeared in front of him before, hurries people up in the most extraordinary way. Sometimes you will be standing on your feet making your submission and the judge is getting up and going for the door to go think about it before you've even finished. It's perfectly proper, of course, for Your Honours to look at the issue of getting a move on. No one would wish to gainsay that, but that cannot, we submit, extend to fettering the discretion of counsel who are charged with the defence of their client, fettering that discretion to choose which witnesses are called. In our respectful submission, the desire of Your Honours to say we will choose which witnesses you may call is one which is not based on a proper application of Article 21 which is, I'm afraid, as I described it earlier, not optional.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: May I say a few things? You have to draw a distinction between eyewitnesses and other witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The statute doesn't make such a distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: -- it might come down to that are we bound to hear the same evidence thrice, four times, five times, six times?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If you had set up such a regime at the beginning of this trial, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That's what I said. Draw a distinction between the eyewitnesses and other witnesses. I don't think there's any law which forces us to hear the same evidence on the same issue more than twice, thrice, four times. With what you said, as regards to which witness you want to produce, you're free to do that. We're not here to tell you which witness to examine and which witness to examine on a particular point. That is entirely your discretion. You can always -- the Belgian principles, as far as the Belgian law is concerned, they are perfectly right and I am entirely in support of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Does the Prosecution have any contribution? If they do, we'll hear them and then we'll find out.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Your Honour, the Prosecution would first note that it's not entirely clear what is being disputed here. I think there is absolutely no dispute that counsel, be they for the Defence or the Prosecution, are entitled to present their case. It's also, I think, beyond dispute that Your Honours have the right, indeed, the duty to control the courtroom and to prevent irrelevant or unnecessarily duplicative testimony. Further, as far as I know, Your Honours have not told the Defence attorneys that they cannot call a particular witness. That being said, we're not sure exactly what the particular issue is. The Prosecution does not agree that different rules are being applied for the Prosecution and the Defence. As Mr. Greaves pointed out, there were instances where the Prosecution was not entitled to call witnesses, either because Your Honours felt we had not adequately given good cause or because Your Honours found the proffer of the testimony to be irrelevant. We can also note in the Prosecution's case the Defence had very detailed witness statements of what the witnesses were going to testify to. So to the extent there was going to be irrelevant or unnecessarily duplicative evidence, that could be raised by the Defence. It may well be that in this case where Your Honours are trying, correctly, to move things along, to ask for more detailed proffers from the Defence attorney. Certainly, it's also the case that Your Honours and other judges can put time limits, put limits on the numbers, any number of things. That being said, that Your Honours certainly have power to control the courtroom, we would also agree that there are some disputed matters and that there is a fine line between cumulative testimony and corroboration, particularly where credibility of the witnesses is in issue. Again, the Prosecution would point out that both the Prosecution and Defence have been prevented from exploring certain areas because Your Honours found it to be irrelevant or duplicative. Obviously, Your Honours have rights. We do agree that with respect to matters that are very important and are contested, some leeway needs to be given to all sides to explore those issues. That's all we have to say, Your Honour, unless you have any specific questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No, no, nothing particularly. Yes, Mr. Greaves, if you have something to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: One recalls both Dr. Calic and Dr. Gow covered, in part, similar ground. They are not victims. I note that my learned friend speaks about witnesses not being allowed to discuss matters which were irrelevancies. I have conceded that Your Honours plainly have the power to prevent irrelevant evidence, indeed, probably the duty to prevent irrelevant evidence. That is so, I suspect, in every legal system that exists. The example that I picked out about the handwriting expert was to show that there were specific, proper reasons unrelated to Your Honours descending into the arena. The point is this: The statute is there. It says what it says. The regime has been set up for the Prosecution. It should be the same for the Defence. It's the level playing field. That's all we ask, a level playing field, no more and no less than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Your witnesses will be treated in the same fashion as the witnesses for the Prosecution. You have the same rights regarding the production of evidence as the Prosecution, but we can always control duplication, triplication, quadruplication of evidence. I'm trying to draw a distinction between eyewitnesses and other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Greaves, I'm not interrupting you, I'm just trying to ensure that there are two differences of approach in terms of proceedings generally, whether criminal or civil. The perception of relevance or irrelevance, to a large extent, depends on how particular counsel sees his or her defence. Now, we have always relied on both Articles 20 and 21, and we can see the expedition which Article 20 expects the Trial Chamber to observe and the doing of justice to the accused persons. If you compare that with the unlimited right to call witnesses, whether relevant or irrelevant, or to tender evidence, even if it is conflicting or irrelevant, cannot stand with the right of the Trial Chamber to manage the case presented to it. Now, when you talk about unrestricted right to call evidence and tender whatever testimony you think, in your own perception, is relevant, you are sometimes treading on the toes of expedition under Article 20 which is still not right. It is the Trial Chamber which is the guardian of that particular provision, not counsel. Perhaps it is forgotten in the doing of justice, the Trial Chamber has a duty to the accused persons, to counsel and to all parties in the case. The moment you start assuming or having a perception that there is inequality or perception and that the Trial Chamber is having a different view in respect of one case, then you get into trouble of thinking that things are going against you. Sometime I'll ask counsel and, perhaps very wrongly, I'll say to look at their case again, look at it afresh and see whether they are doing the right thing. They should look at the indictment again, look at the evidence against them and see where they are going. It is the duty of the Trial Chamber to do that. We do not leave the management of the case to counsel, because counsel himself is not an impartial participator in the whole proceedings. It is our duty to do what we are doing. Now, you talked about Article 21. You cannot for one moment suggest to anybody that there is no unrestricted rights to call witnesses. You can't say that. The parity which you ascribe to both parties exists and the parity is not compared on a general, neutral plain. It is compared on the type of proceedings which each one is trying to develop before the Trial Chamber, that they should be given the same right, the same opportunities. That does not mean that one should abuse his own right because he is allowed to call evidence. That is not the issue. The interpretation has not been exhausted, I know. There are a few cases which have interpreted it, but every situation has its own interpretation. It's not the same for all. You've compared the Prosecution with the Defence. Obviously it can never be the same. The Prosecution has a global case to make against four persons. Each accused has a case to make on his own defence, so how do you put the two together? You see, there are very few things which goes beyond practise. It comes with theory as a whole, the theory of judicial administration, the theory of the way the court administers matters before it. But one thing you will have, as long as one's decision is not based on his whims, merely on one's caprice, no matter what Article 21(4)(e) says, it cannot be a violation. It cannot be a violation that someone decides to call a witness who is not even referring to the issue merely because counsel thinks that an analogy can be drawn. If you think that sufficient evidence has been given and has been admitted in respect of what has been argued, obviously surplus does not improve the quality of evidence given. Nobody is saying that you should not call your witnesses, but you should call your witnesses who are relevant to the case and who will give admissible evidence. That is what the Trial Chamber is saying. In fact, perhaps one might consider this. It is the Prosecution which should be concerned that one is going to the assistance of the Defence by helping him to trim down his own witnesses. They should be angry, not for the Defence, which has taken on the advantage of that extra effort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Take your own client's case. The first list submitted was of 365 witnesses. The Trial Chamber had the right to know --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: He's actually my former client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Your former client, I beg your pardon. With 365, don't you think the Trial Chamber has the right to know what these witnesses are going to say? The allegation against you is your command and responsibility with regard to Celebici camp, what allegedly happened in Celebici camp. Now, if you start producing witnesses who have no relation at all to Celebici, who can throw no light on what this camp was and what your precise duties there were, if there were any, how interested in the other evidence? Now interpret Article 20 of the statute. Are we bound to hear everyone he produces who says nothing about what actually happened in Celebici camp and he had no relation to those acts? You're also talking about an expeditious trial. We're talking about a fair trial. We are only interested in the evidence which relates to the issue against you, the charges against you. We aren't interested in hearing all the evidence of the 365 who probably have never even heard of Celebici. Therefore, we wanted to know what those witnesses are going to say. What is their evidence going to be relevant for for our purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm not going to comment on a witness list that's been submitted by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You're saying that we are choosing the witnesses. We are not choosing the witnesses. Choose your own witnesses. All we say, don't duplicate, don't triplicate, and you don't even have to prove facts which are given by the Prosecution witnesses themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: One of the difficulties we face is this: We can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We have not chosen any witnesses. We just said produce your evidence, but it should be relevant and don't duplicate. Then we said, so far as eyewitnesses are concerned, they are in a different position. Well, if you have any eyewitnesses, please produce them and we will examine them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Of course I hear what Your Honour says. We're faced with looking at the transcript which says this: "Now, as I said what the Trial Chamber intends to do is come up with our own list of witnesses," and so one can be forgiven for thinking that Your Honours intended to choose for the Defence which witnesses were to be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are correct. I said that; I did. I thought I was being of assistance to the whole exercise, to make sure that things are properly done in the interests of the accused persons themselves. But if you look at it very carefully, if you look at the synthesis of both the type of practise we are applying here, the Trial Chamber is properly entitled even to do that. It is entitled. Forget your legal arguments. They might sound interesting, but definitely go back, think about the two philosophies which have been matched in our procedure. You will find that we are perfectly entitled to do that in the interests of Article 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We have not done that so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No, we have not, but we are perfectly entitled --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We just asked counsel to cut down the list, if possible, so that duplication, triplication are avoided.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If that's as far as it goes, then, of course, nobody could have any exception to it. But it may be that counsel, out of a sense of over anxiety for his client, does call somebody who Your Honours think is duplication. Of course, one of the problems is that we can't see into Your Honours' minds and we don't know what decision you have taken about any particular witness, whether you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You have the evidence before you when you examine the witness. You know you are examining a certain person on such and such an issue or you examine two witnesses or three witnesses on that. You know that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The Prosecution may challenge that evidence, and until Your Honours come to a final judgement, we don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This is what we object to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: -- which witness -- sorry, the evidence of which witness you accept. Do you accept the Prosecution version of that or the Defence? So we can't see into Your Honours' minds and know with accuracy which evidence you accept so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You put the administration into the extra expense of bringing down, in respect of each of the accused persons, the same witness. This is what happens. So if for one thing which, perhaps, one or two witnesses could do, you have caused the administration to pay for about eight or more witnesses. That is grossly undesirable. If, perhaps, you are paying your own fees, if the accused persons themselves are paying for it, they would not want to do it. Nobody would have been paying for duplicated evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If you'll just give me a moment, I have just had something drawn to my attention and I'd just like to read it, please, before I open my mouth again and say something unwise. Would you just give me a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Perhaps you should have it very clear in your mind that what we are avoiding is waste of funds; waste of time. Both, cumulatively. Because the moment you call duplicated witnesses, it extends the time for trial. It increases the funds spent for the trial. It just doesn't make sense. In fact, when I consider it very carefully, very few lawyers, counsel would like to duplicate this, the witnesses, you wouldn't, because of the obvious risks involved in duplicated witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That's right, one tries to, where possible to avoid duplication. Let's take for example, one's own experience of, for example, a pub brawl which ends up with the participants being --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Eyewitnesses, you're talking eyewitnesses. We'll not stop you from producing any eyewitnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Those are both eyewitnesses, but then there are, of course, the police officers who attend the scene afterwards. You may well find yourself or other bystanders who do not witness the event, but the aftermath or some other thing, one certainly calls people who duplicate evidence and do not get criticised for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You're comparing general principle with actual cases before us. We're dealing with the particular matter before us. I know the effect of what it could be and there's no point arguing it at length.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to go on, I hate going on at length. What concerns us is that we cannot see into Your Honours' minds and know what you've accepted it. And if it's challenged by the Prosecution, although there is no general requirement for corroboration, there is no doubt that if three or more people confirm some thing, then they can support one another in the acceptance in that testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: As I said the other day, it's not the number of witnesses, it's the quality of the evidence that is more important. As experienced counsel, you know that what will carry weight and what will not carry weight. For example, on a particular issue, you produce a man who is really responsible or who is probably head of the whole thing and then you try to corroborate a reply, proper evidence. If you don't read the manners directly, who has the direct knowledge, how would you expect the other witnesses who do not have that knowledge to talk about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Here we have same cases in talking about the authority, role on authority and responsibility of a particular officer. You have a chief of staff of that same particular officer. You have the authority appointing him. You still have to find another officer of a different jurisdiction and, in turn, to bring some officers of that jurisdiction. What is the relevance? Especially in respect of the authority of that, where in fact the appointing authority has already given evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I proffer a final example?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I hope you got the point. Duplication and triplication doesn't help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That's what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I have heard all what Your Honours say. Can I just give one last example? Which may assist Your Honours to see where the difficulties may arise. The Prosecution has a witness who deals with a matter for the first time. They cross-examine that witness and suggest that he's not telling the truth or that he's made some inconsistent prior statement. You can't just leave it there. If there's another witness who deals with that same point, it is the duty of the Defence to call that witness, so that that witness may support and demonstrate that the first witness, contrary to what the Prosecution has said, is, in fact, a truthful, accurate and reliable witness. In the absence of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You might have produced two conflicting Defence witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I am anticipating and hope that when the second witness is called, they don't deviate from that which is anticipated. That's the example that I give to demonstrate why the process may be thought by counsel, who, of course, doesn't know what Your Honours have accepted, feels it necessary to call their second witness as to the same point. That's the problem. Your Honours may seek to say this is duplication and, therefore, --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Triplication, quadruplication --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Saying the same thing. We've heard the arguments. We've heard what the Defence objects to. We'll stay within the guidelines which the law allows us to apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I have made my submissions and I urge them upon Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my learned colleague has articulated all our arguments. However, Judge Jan has asked one question and in relation to that question, I would kindly ask Your Honours to permit me to state my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: My fear is that we would descending and discussing the case which we have and I do not intend doing that. You've made your objections and we've had them. We've indicated application of the rules as we have them, so it doesn't really matter. Let's not discuss the case which is on hand. It's already at hand so why do you discuss it?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My comment does not have to do with the argumentation because I fully support what colleague Greaves has said. But only it has to do with equal treatment of all witnesses, regardless of whether they are victims or not. This is a question that has not been discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We don't have to discuss the quality on that. Thank you very much. Now the next motion is for leave to call expert witnesses. Now, I really don't know why you want about eight expert witnesses for Landzo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is he a historian?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, historian. We are the only defendant accused in the Tribunal alleging an affirmative Defence of some sort, lack of mental capacity and diminished physical ability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Nobody has accused him of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honour, that's a Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You still have a Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What I mean by that, you have abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: The only one we abandoned was alibi, Your Honour. Therefore, 50% of our case rests upon expert testimony. Therefore, we have listed, first of all, many of the doctors listed had examined Mr. Landzo a long time ago. They are coming from prior examinations and they have known him through the period of 1992. Three of the doctors were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You mean his childhood doctor?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: One of them was a paediatrician, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He was born with some disability?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It was a congenital problem and we feel it's necessary. And I have taken, if you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No matter what is what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Produce your witnesses and we'll see how far they're relevant when they come.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I have already from the original list that I gave, I have taken several of the experts off. I really do feel that the ones that I have asked to be designated are necessary. I would also like the court to be aware and ask that this be accepted now as a supplement to my motion for designation. I just received it from my investigator. It is something that resembles, a curriculum vitae, but it no way arises to that. These are the doctors from the Konjic municipality. If I could, here are the three copies for the Court, a copy for the Registry and the Prosecution has already been provided a copy, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We'd be interested in his mental condition at the time when the offences are committed, not before, not after.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Have the doctors speak about that. Fair enough, we'll examine them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That is, I am limiting to the time of the allegations in the indictment to 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Because the law, as I understand it, you may be insane before and you may be insane afterwards --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There's no such defence of insanity available.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I am aware of that. That is where I am limiting the Defence to the time in 1992. Are there any further questions, because I am asking leave of court to designate these witnesses now. And if they're so designated -- I see that Ms. McHenry, of course, would like to respond to this. Would you like to go ahead? I'll respond to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: The Prosecution would certainly like to respond before Your Honours take this matter under consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Would you like to file a response or just reply now?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Why don't I just reply now and if Your Honours think it would be helpful for us to supplement with a written response, we're happy to do so. As far back as January, 1997, Your Honours directed everyone to give notice of expert witnesses and to give certain information about them. Not only has the Defence of Mr. Esad Landzo not done that, to be perfectly frank, the Prosecution still does not even understand what all the affirmative defences are. I am raising this now for two reasons: One is to prevent the unnecessary expenditure of time and money by various bodies of the Tribunal, including the Prosecution. The other one is to save time, to make sure that the Prosecution can be adequately prepared for this defence in advance so that we are not caught by surprise, such that we then have to ask for some sort of lengthy recess to prepare. Given that these are very specialised matters that we are talking about, and let me be very frank, the Prosecution bench does not include any psychiatrists or medical doctors. So, these are very specialised areas. For that reason, we think we may need more information than would be necessary if we knew, in effect, what was going on. I will give just one example. The defence of diminished physical impairment. It is hard for the Prosecution to believe that the Defence is, that because of his asthma and because of an injury to two fingers, Mr. Landzo was incapable of committing the acts with which he is charged. If that is not the Defence, if that's not what they're stating, then we would argue that the evidence is entirely irrelevant. If it is their argument that he could not have committed the acts with which he is charged because his physical impairments were so severe, then certainly the Prosecution is going to have to undertake its own investigation and, presumably, it its own examination. We have been reluctant to request additional experts and to do all that when it seems so unlikely that, in fact, this is going to be what the exact Defence is. Certainly with respect to the physical impairment, we would be asking for further details about the nature of the Defence and the nature of what the Defence experts would testify to. A one sentence description that medical doctor or paediatrician who treated Mr. Landzo for respiratory problems, does not under these circumstances give the Prosecution sufficient information with which we could even prepare for cross-examination. We fear this will cause a lengthy delay later on and because we haven't wanted to do that, is why we filed the motion a few months earlier, asking that they provide more precision. We think that they have not adequately complied with Your Honours' ruling. Similarly, let me go on to another issue, which is Dr. Gripon. In the recent filing by the Defence of Esad Landzo, the defence indicates that Mr. Gripon may not produce an expert report, but that, in any event, he will be relying upon, and I now quote, "Upon his personal interviews with Mr. Landzo, his family, his friends, soldiers from Celebici camp and other persons familiar with his personal environment in 1992". Again, for the Prosecution to be able to examine Dr. Gripon, we would have to have access well in advance to the material relied on by Dr. Gripon in coming up with his evaluation. We'd be asking Your Honours to order the Defence to provide to the Prosecution, the material relied upon by Dr. Gripon in forming his expert opinion by June 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We ask counsel to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Then, just finally, the Prosecution notes that the Defence historian, although he's a historian, he is scheduled to testify about the psychology of ethnic groups and individuals caught up on the war and international humanitarian law. Again, the Prosecution is unclear whether this person is being called as a historian or as a psychologist or even the relevance of this. So, in order that the Prosecution can be prepared for this Defence and so that this trial is not delayed further, we would be asking Your Honour to direct the Defence to provide a significant amount of additional information at the present time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: May I respond to Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I think that the Prosecution has stipulated that they have received ample notice of our intention of calling Dr. Gripon and the other experts that I have listed. What they are complaining about is that I have not provided a report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: And that you're not likely to provide one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: That I may not. First of all, I don't believe that any decision or order of this Trial Chamber or any rule of evidence or any rule of procedure in the statute requires us to have a report made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Not you, the experts.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the expert, asked for me to request that they make one. But if there is an existing report that we are relying on, that we have a duty to disclose it to the Prosecution. I agree with that. Number one, they called Professor Economides and Dr. Gow without supplying us any expert report before these experts testified. They did not ask for a report from these experts. If I don't choose to have a report written, then I believe my explanation, which satisfies the court's order of January, 1997, which says that we give them a description of the area that they will be testifying about. I believe that page 3 of the designation of expert witnesses gives a description of what it is Dr. Gripon will testify to, what he replies upon in forming his testimony, the evidence that he will give. Also going on now to the part about the Defence of diminished physical capacity. It's listed there that he has an injury to his two right fingers that makes them useless and also that he has a congenital respiratory problem. The only thing-- Ms. McHenry is absolutely correct, that is the Defence of lack of mental capacity. The witnesses came here. They said that someone was beaten 200 times with a baseball bat for five hours. We have a right to bring experts to say that it would not have been possible for that defendant to do that. That is the basis of that defence. It was, I think, even though it wasn't spelled out before, it was quite clear in what it was that we alleged what his injuries were and from the testimony of the Prosecution witnesses. Therefore, I believe that the only non-compliance that the Prosecution can complain of at this point is that we did not provide a report of Dr. Gripon. Dr. Gripon will either be here tomorrow or next Thursday to complete his evaluation of Mr. Landzo. When he completes his evaluation, I may or may not ask him to write a report. If I do ask him to write a report, I will most certainly supply it to the Prosecution as soon as I receive it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May I just clarify. The Prosecution is not stating that every expert witness has to provide an expert report. I'm sorry if Defence counsel took it that way. The Prosecution is stating that the Defence has to give the prosecution adequate notice of the substance of the testimony and an opportunity to review the material relied upon by the expert. Now sometimes that happens by way of an expert report, but we're not saying it is necessary. But with respect to Dr. Gripon, we'd certainly be asking for a more detailed description of what his testimony is going to be, rather than just the mental health of the accused. We would be asking for the opportunity to review the material which he relied on, be they interviews with other people, be they medical reports, et cetera. That's with respect to -- we are not objecting to the calling of Dr. Gripon or the other three mental health professionals for whom we've received notice some time ago and for whom we have expert reports. We are objecting, though, to the manner in which we have been advised and the specifics we have been given about the physical impairment Defence, as well as the historian who is going to talk about the psychology of ethnic groups. So I won't repeat what I was going to say, I just want to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If my understanding of Dr. Gripon's expertise is correct, I think he's only coming to discuss matters relating to physical disability or his capacity to commit the acts which the accused has been charged.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I think Dr. Gripon -- Ms. McMurrey will correct me -- but Dr. Gripon is the fourth mental health expert they wish to call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mental health too?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, he is a forensic psychiatrist. He is the, really the main expert. He has been on the case evaluating Mr. Landzo since March of last year. He is the forensic expert we're calling. The other doctors that evaluated him prior to, Lagazzi, Loga and van Leeuwen, as through the registry, he is using their material in order to formulate as a basis for his own studies and evaluations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He has no expert for physical disabilities?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: The only experts I am calling for the physical disabilities are the doctors who treated Mr. Landzo in the Konjic area at the time that he was treated, you know, from the time he was born for the respiratory problems and from the time he had the surgery from Dr. Buturovic in 1991 for the fingers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You included the first three specialists, who treated him first?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You've included the first three specialists, Loga and the team. They are also included?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: In addition to Gripon who is using their report?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have four psychiatrists, mental health experts to call. Because this is really the first time a lack of mental capacity Defence has been used in a war crimes trial. I feel that each one has just a little something different to say about their perception, whether it goes to PTSD or whether it goes to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I mean he's using the reports of the others and then basing it on his own.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are all of the others also experts?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, the others are also experts, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is he a super expert above all of them?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: He's a forensic psychologist, there's a difference. I mean psychiatrist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: My understanding of medical experts may be a little old-fashioned, I suppose, but I believe the law is very clear on what is medical evidence on the state of a person's mental health.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I think it's clear in Texas, and it may be clear in Nigeria. I am not quite sure how clear it is here yet. I feel that these four experts are necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Now we have also motions for protective measures, which Delalic has brought. Ms. McHenry, have you been served with the motion for protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: We were served with them during the lunch break and I have not yet had an opportunity to read them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Perhaps we might be able to take them tomorrow, if possible. We'll take them tomorrow morning. The Trial Chamber will now rise. I think we'll reassemble tomorrow morning at ten.
